title: A mental model for great teaching
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart's subject is not what great teaching is but how what we know about it should be organised in teachers' heads. Ask anyone what makes great teaching and you get a list, and lists grow until they are unwieldy and unmemorable - a problem he illustrates with Rosenshine's seventeen principles, which experienced teachers can mentally order but novices cannot. He walks up a ladder of organisation: simple chunking, as in AERO's four groups; broader conceptual dimensions, as in Evidence Based Education's Great Teaching Toolkit; and Mary Kennedy's parsing of teaching as five persistent problems to be solved. His own proposal layers strategies beneath the problems they solve and beneath propositions - generalised, evidence-based truths about teaching and learning - so that think-pair-share is held not as an isolated tactic but as one solution to directing attention, which matters because children learn only what they attend to. The payoff he claims is twofold: organised knowledge makes teacher CPD meaningful rather than rote, and shared organisation gives colleagues a common language for collaboration. It also offers an escape from what he calls the consistency trap, where leaders mandate a strategy because research says so and erode teacher agency. The final section adds judgement: a mental model, as distinct from a schema, represents the decision process of choosing among options and knowing when not to use a strategy at all.
points: Hart's central claim is that defining great teaching is a communication and improvement problem, not a theoretical one, so the organisation of the knowledge matters as much as its content.

Rosenshine's seventeen principles are used as the worked example of the list problem: an expert can impose order on them, which is precisely why they are least useful to the novice who needs the order supplied.

The proposition-problem-strategy stack is the transferable idea - anchoring each strategy in the problem it solves and the reason that problem deserves attention is what turns CPD from rote to meaningful.
He names the consistency trap directly: mandating a practice because research says erodes agency and decision making, whereas anchoring it in problems lets teachers judge when it applies.
The distinction between a schema and a mental model is judgement - the model adds choosing among options and knowing when not to deploy a strategy, with conditional if-clauses attached to each.
quotes: The question of what makes great teaching rightly occupies the minds of teachers and school leaders. It is the quality of teaching that makes the biggest difference to children’s learning followed by the leadership required to create the conditions for great teaching to happen.

If you ponder on your own or ask any teacher What makes great teaching?, you inevitably get a list. And the more we think, the longer that list grows. Long lists are unwieldy and therefore difficult to remember and this is important.

The whole point of defining great teaching has to be to be able to communicate it clearly and help teachers to improve. Defining great teaching is not a theoretical exercise, it should be a priority for teachers interested in getting better and leaders interested in school improvement to drive CPD and improve children’s learning.

A proposition is an evidence based truth about teaching or learning that is altogether more generalised than anything we might have on list of what makes great teaching. This is fundamental to meaningful learning (in this case, teacher CPD) because what we are able to learn hinges on what we already know, otherwise learning is rote.

They know the strategy think, pair share but have organised it in a way that shows it is a way of solving the problem of directing children’s attention. And we know this is a worthy problem for teachers to think about solutions to because children can only learn what they pay attention to.

The key difference is judgement. A mental model represents the decision making process that we need teachers to go through. Judgement is required if we are going to achieve coherence over consistency and ensure teacher agency.
